drills.q: What's the corpus-level question, as opposed to the single-skill question?
drills.a: Does the whole corpus stay one coherent system as it grows -- composition, collisions, shared invariants -- not just does any one skill fire correctly.

drills.q: Roughly what does one skill's listing entry cost in tokens?
drills.a: About 100 tokens (name + description), paid every session regardless of whether it's used.

drills.q: Name the four skill composition patterns.
drills.a: Serial, parallel, conditional routing, and recursive/nested invocation.

drills.q: Which composition pattern scales best and why?
drills.a: Serial composition through a shared artifact on disk -- it doesn't require one skill to know another exists, only that both agree on the artifact's shape.

drills.q: Name the corpus-scale failure mode where two skills each pass their own trigger test individually.
drills.a: Description collision -- the same or similar prompt fires a different skill on different sessions because their vocabularies now overlap.

drills.q: How do you detect description collision across a corpus?
drills.a: Run every skill's should-trigger prompts against the WHOLE corpus and flag any prompt that fires more than one skill.

drills.q: How does composition/collision risk scale with corpus size?
drills.a: Combinatorially -- n skills yield up to n(n-1)/2 possible pairwise compositions, and the same arithmetic for pairwise collisions.

drills.q: In this repo's reference architecture, what is the fragments-not-aggregates invariant and what does it buy?
drills.a: Every content-writing skill writes its own fragment file rather than hand-editing generated aggregates; a build step merges by id, letting many independently-invoked skills run in any order with no race.

drills.q: What is the weakest link in this repo's fragments-not-aggregates invariant?
drills.a: It's enforced by README convention only, not by code -- Level 1 instruction, not Level 3 enforcement; nothing stops a new skill from hand-editing the aggregate directly.

drills.q: Why does a skill's cost model change inside a forked subagent?
drills.a: A subagent's preloaded skills inject full content at startup rather than following the regular session's progressive name+description listing -- a cheap skill in the main session can be a real cold-start cost once nested.

drills.q: Is a marketplace with hundreds of thousands of community skills a quality signal?
drills.a: No -- it's adoption evidence for the format, not a quality or safety signal for any individual skill in the pool.

drills.q: When is a skill-mediated architecture the wrong corpus-level design?
drills.a: When most capability is unconditional (belongs in a rules file) or deterministic-and-fragile (belongs in scripts/tools) -- padding a corpus with misclassified content dilutes listing budget for the skills that actually need progressive disclosure.
